Tough.question: Synthesizing the concepts of principal quantum number (n), shielding, and nuclear charge, why does the atomic radius expansion per step down Group 1 (alkali metals: Li->Na is +34 pm, Na->K is +45 pm, K->Rb is +13 pm, Rb->Cs is +18 pm) exhibit variations rather than a uniform increase, even though size generally increases?

Tough.question: Consider the species S^2-, Cl-, K+, and Ca^2+. Which of the following correctly describes their radius relationships?

options.A: They are not isoelectronic, so no radius comparison can be made.
options.B: They are isoelectronic with 18 electrons; hence their radii decrease in the order S^2- > Cl- > K+ > Ca^2+ due to increasing nuclear charge.
options.C: Their radii increase in the order S^2- < Cl- < K+ < Ca^2+.
options.D: Their radii are all exactly equal because they have the same number of electrons.

Tough.explanation: S^2- (Z=16), Cl- (Z=17), K+ (Z=19), and Ca^2+ (Z=20) each possess 18 electrons. As nuclear charge increases from 16 to 20, the electrostatic attraction on the 18 electrons increases, causing the ionic radius to decrease steadily from S^2- down to Ca^2+.

Tough.question: Consider the isoelectronic series: Ti^4+, V^5+, Cr^6+, and Mn^7+. How do their ionic radii vary, and what is the underlying physical reason?

options.A: Radii increase from Ti^4+ to Mn^7+ because nuclear charge increases.
options.B: Radii decrease from Ti^4+ to Mn^7+ because the effective nuclear charge increases significantly due to increasing atomic number with a constant number of electrons.
options.C: Radii remain completely identical because they have the exact same number of electrons.
options.D: Radii fluctuate randomly depending on the d-orbital occupancy.

Tough.explanation: Ti^4+, V^5+, Cr^6+, and Mn^7+ are all isoelectronic (each has 10 electrons, having lost all their valence electrons to attain noble gas configurations). As atomic number increases from 22 (Ti) to 25 (Mn), the nuclear charge increases while the electron cloud remains the same size (10 electrons), pulling the cloud closer and causing a sharp decrease in ionic radius.

Medium.question: Among second period elements, why does Beryllium (Be) have a higher ionization enthalpy than Boron (B)?

options.A: Boron has a smaller nuclear charge than Beryllium.
options.B: It is easier to remove a 2p electron from Boron than to remove a 2s electron from the fully filled, stable 2s^2 subshell of Beryllium.
options.C: Beryllium is a noble gas.
options.D: Boron forms covalent bonds which shield its valence electrons completely.

The single 2p electron in Boron is shielded by the inner core and 2s electrons, making it easier to remove than a 2s electron from Beryllium, resulting in a lower ionization enthalpy for Boron.

Medium.question: Why do noble gases exhibit very low chemical reactivity?

options.A: They have high electron gain enthalpies.
options.B: All orbitals in their valence shell are completely filled with an ns2np6 configuration, making it difficult to alter.
options.C: They readily lose their outer electrons.
options.D: They form predominantly ionic compounds easily.
